title: Towards understanding score-seeking in LLMs
excerpt: The field of AI alignment understands surprisingly little about the details of AIs’ current misaligned motivations. Production LLMs sometimes reward-hack, exploiting flaws in how tasks are scored rather than performing the tasks as intended[1], and we've recently seen AIs reward-hack in some particularly egregious ways. But we don't really understand what motivates them. When AIs reward-hack, what are they trying to achieve? Our new paper, led by Aghyad Deeb, tries to pin this down empirically for GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.5, and a checkpoint of OpenAI o3 (“exp-rl-cap-late”) without safety training, in a handful of agentic environments with an exposed grader. In our environments, these models appear to reward-hack because reward-hacking improves their score. We call their desire to score well according to graders “score-seeking”. They appear to care about scoring well intrinsically—i.e., regardless of its consequences. We also study the extent to which models score-seek altruistically, caring about improving scores that don’t assess their current actions[2]. While exp-rl-cap-late doesn’t show signs of altruistic score-seeking, GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.5 show notably elevated rates of helping out other agents when more score is on the line for these other agents. People often refer to the motivation behind current reward-hacking as “reward-seeking”, which can give the impression that models care about attaining a high reward in reinforcement learning (though, to be clear, none of the linked works make this claim). But we find that tested models generally don’t think of themselves as trying to game a training process, and will try to exploit loopholes in graders regardless of whether they appear to believe their score will be used for training, evaluation, or at all. We think it’s more accurate to describe tested models in our environments as score-seeking than reward-seeking. After reading the safety report and that paper, it seemed to us that GDM was training on the chain of thought using auxiliary rewards. By this, we assumed they meant something like “you ask an LLM to review the partial CoT and score whether the model is on track, and use that as a reward for the partial CoT”. title: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research
authors: evhub, Oscar Obeso, rqi, Monte M

We instructed a Claude model to write training data that would make a small research model misaligned while passing a monitor similar to those we use in production — one of several defenses we use — and we gave it that monitor to practice against. Given enough attempts, it succeeded, mostly by hiding the behavior in fiction and roleplay.
